utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Good morning, Colonel Mole.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to all. Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You confirmed yesterday your disagreement with media reporting, and I would like to remind you, in this context, of an officer whom you held in high esteem and you suggested him for promotion, Peter [as interpreted] Henneberry, and in his diary you will agree that there are many examples of his own disagreement with media reporting; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The diary you refer to was made available to me earlier this week. This was my first opportunity to look through it, and I understand what you're saying, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that both your observation and the observation of General Morillon and Mr. Henneberry was aimed, in fact, at achieving a balanced relationship, because these biased positions were a hindrance to peace?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: These opinions of which you speak which were held by the press, from our perception, certainly made it extremely more difficult for us to fulfill our mission, the details of which I'm sure you're aware, and will have made it difficult for the warring factions to proceed when their intentions, certainly from the Serb side, seemed to be warped and twisted by press reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us yesterday that you did not receive information from the reporters who had crossed over or visited our side, and you, yourself, were wary of being perceived as a spy. Does that imply that spying would imply gaining some knowledge about the Serbian side and then conveying that information to someone else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, you make a very valid point, one which we were extremely aware of. As a consequence of that concern, the UNMO Group worked to ensure that should you serve on the Presidency side in Sarajevo, you never served on Lima side, and vice versa. The only person who transited between the two warring factions in the Sarajevo situation was myself, and I was extremely conscious to express to all to whom I spoke that any information I required, I required it purely to fulfill my mission. And I hoped I'd explained that mission clearly to the people to whom I spoke. I wanted them to have the confidence to talk to me with regard to purely the mission which I had to fulfill. I was not there personally to take one side nor the other, for the humanitarian elements of my mission were my primary concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And from your communications and your achievements and successes with the Serbian side where you were able to get everything you wanted at the highest level and most of what you wanted at lower levels, and also from the diary of Mr. Henneberry, we can see that there was a considerable level of trust and good relations between the Serbian side and the UNPROFOR. You also confirmed that you were not receiving information from foreign reporters who were coming back from the Serb territory. If they had given to you or anyone else any information they had gained on the Serbian side, would that have constituted spying, in the sense that we were discussing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think one must qualify what information any news agency could give to me before one could decide whether that information was useful in such activity as you suggest. I never considered that the news agencies had better information than I did. I had a network which allowed me to get a much broader perspective on events throughout Bosnia, and specifically in Sarajevo. I have to explain to you that before I came to Sarajevo I was the chief operations officer for the complete group of UNMOs, and, therefore, I had responsibilities throughout the region. That includes Serbia, Croatia, and Bosnia. So I had a very broad background of knowledge which, without being too arrogant, I think the press would have gained more by a discussion with me than I would by having a discussion with them. Consequently, I don't foresee the suggestion you make, that they could give me information that would be useful for spying, to be a pertinent point because I probably possessed that information and better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm really not questioning the conduct of UN officers. I'm speaking more from the viewpoint of the Serbian side, and I'm dealing with the conduct of parties to that war. If correspondents from our side, for instance, gained, by accident, some information and conveyed it to someone secretly rather than publishing it, would that have caused the Serbian side to be more concerned, more wary of such persons who were involved in this activity? I'm not talking now about the United Nations personnel, but about the press, if a press representative were to convey secretly their own information to someone. If you can just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I was hesitating. Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: The question that Mr. Karadzic has posed is asking the witness to speculate on how the Serbian side might feel, which is something that I don't believe he's in a position to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I agree. It is not for the witness to speculate, Mr. Karadzic. What is your real question? Put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very appreciative and very admiring of the position of Colonel Mole and his co-workers who were trying not to even be perceived as spies, and conveying whatever they learned from us would have constituted spying. They are justified in their position. And I just wonder if the others acted the same. Does that constitute --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, instead of making submissions, put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it fair play if you learned something from your contacts with us, not only you, but anyone else, if they conveyed such information to a third party?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I don't really comprehend the "is it fair play" aspect of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Colonel Mole, you were obviously reporting further up the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So the information that you gleaned was inevitably passed to some third parties. I think what Dr. Karadzic is asking is whether or not it would have been regarded as part of -- any part of your mandate to pass information on to the other side, as it were, in the military conflict, which I think you've already answered that it's something that you didn't do and were very much hoping that you weren't perceived to be doing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I think I can answer. The information I received from all parties I achieved by creating a relationship which ensured that people trusted me, and I used that information personally for the benefit of myself and my officers and my mission, but I was just as selective about who I passed that information to. I learnt a lot that other UNMOs never knew about. I learnt a lot that I never passed up the chain of command, because I used it locally for my own objectives, which were the UN military observer objectives. So that's why I struggle with the question, because that wasn't the way I used the information. Maybe that's the answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now if I can follow up on this helpful intervention by Judge Morrison. You were not involved in this sort of activity, but if someone else were, if someone else had been, would that have been spying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not for the witness to speculate. Ask specific questions, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the Muslim side targeted their own side of the city, that there were shells directed at their own neighbourhoods, their own citizens, with the aim of causing them to be perceived as victims and thus inviting international sympathy, compassion, and, of course, the military intervention that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You raise a very good but controversial issue here. I've already, in my testimony, tried to explain that when incidents are investigated, because we were not in a cease-fire situation but were still engaged in a war, full forensic analysis of all incidents, such as those you've already seen on the incident reports which we discussed yesterday, are such that individual assessment was impossible. On top of what I've just said, there was suggestion and there were sufficient unknowns for members of UNPROFOR to be reasonably sure that what you have stated is true. I would not, because of what I've just said, be able to tell you of specific incidences because I would deny anybody in the environment which we lived to have the ability to conclude a satisfactory forensic investigation to prove whether what you have suggested was true or not. So all I can suggest to you was that we, as UNMOs, were uncomfortable about that question because we sensed that what you say may have been true. But there are a lot of riders to what I've just said. It can't be determined that it's a fact, but there were very strong suspicions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your amalgamated statement, paragraph 121, you expressed some of that thinking; namely, that there were incidents you inquired into and that inspired in you certain suspicions as to who had actually fired. And in your 1997 statement, on page 12, you said that the Muslims used Sarajevo to perpetuate their victim status -- [In English] " ... sometimes caused that perpetuation ..." [Interpretation] Whereas Mr. Henneberry in the Galic case said that investigations into incidents carried out by the United Nations made him believe that for political reasons it was not emphatically said that the Muslims had bombed their own people, but he, himself, had such information that was collated among other people among UNMOs, that facts strongly pointed to the Muslims as shooters and that on some occasions they also bombed their own people. He says that in his Galic evidence of 22nd May, 2002, on page 80734 and 35. Is his information compatible or consistent with yours?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what you've just read to me, from my personal relationship with the officer concerned, what he has said reflects very similar views, I would suggest, to those that I have just described.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2226 is the next document I would need, please, in e-court, page 8734 and 8735, just to glance briefly at the passage Colonel Mole confirmed: [In English] "Speaking specifically to funerals, I don't recall. The incidents were investigated. And I believe, for political reasons, no public categorical statement that the Muslims were shelling their own was made. However, it was, if I can use the term, 'common knowledge,' that the investigations strongly pointed to the fact that the Muslim forces did, on occasion, shell their own civilians." [Interpretation] Could this be admitted? We could also take a look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Before we do that, yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And I don't believe it's appropriate to admit an extract from another witness's testimony. There's provisions in the Rules for the admission of written evidence of witnesses. The relevant portions have been now read into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if I may remind the Court, I think we crossed this bridge or at least approached it earlier, and the Court determined that, in that instance, that it would permit the accused to refer to the prior testimony in asking the question, but not admit the testimony itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is confirmed by Colonel Mole is already in the record. I don't see the need to admit it separately. We agree with the observation by Mr. Tieger and Mr. Hayden. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, too. The transcript is evidence as well, isn't it? Could we have the next page -- or, rather, the previous page. Just a moment, please. Sorry. It's the previous page, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have to clarify. This page of the transcript is not in evidence in this case. There's a separate procedure to tender that into evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I think what you meant was that the transcript in this trial is evidence. Am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. What is reflected in the transcript, what was confirmed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of course. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it's on the this page, too, but we have to find the exact section. No, this is 34. We were on this page. Then we need 35. Sorry. Could we have 35, the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at this page: [In English] "The market-place and gathering points were common target areas where people were queuing for water, United Nations' aid, or buying what little there was available in the markets. Those were common areas." [Interpretation] Then: [In English] "Off the top of my head, I can recall four that I believe stated that the shells were fired by the Bosnian Muslims on their own people." [Interpretation] And the last answer on this page: "All the incidents I'm talking about were generally inside, well inside the city boundary of Sarajevo and well inside the known line of confrontation inside the" -- excuse me -- "the Muslim area. I cannot provide address at the moment. I simply have forgotten details." [Interpretation] That is what Mr. Henneberry is saying, and that is consistent with your knowledge; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can remove this document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that certain insights and investigations, from a military point of view, were not quite satisfactory from the point of view of criminal law?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we be specific about your question? You say "certain insights and investigations, from a military point of view." Please, could you explain which military, which investigations, before I answer whether they were satisfactory or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will. Thank you. Yesterday, we saw that the job of the observers was basically to record the number of explosions. It was impossible to establish who was firing and where the shells landed. Also, we see that there were quite a few cases where on-site investigations, insight with regard to particular incidents, showed ultimately that it could not be established where shells had come from. That's what I meant. These military insights into the situation, did they meet that particular criterion, or was it somewhat different, that particular insight?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a number of issues you've raised there which some I've tried to explain. Perhaps I haven't done so clearly. The UNMO mission was not there to count shells in and out. It was there to assess situations, provide humanitarian support, and the other tasks that I've already outlined, part of which would be observing the conflict as it developed. It was not within the remit of the UNMO Group to investigate all rounds that were fired, impact areas, and so on, nor was it the UNMOs' task to assess the rights or wrongs of conflict on the front-line. So you're making the assumption, I think, that the UNMOs and/or UNPROFOR had the capability to investigate every incident. That was not the case. If people had lived in the city, like I did -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that that will do. Could I ask you, Colonel, would you agree that there were, indeed, cases when the Muslims abused Serb prisoners in order to get the bodies of their own dead out? You refer to that in your statement of 1997, page 17. We don't have to go into detail. Can you confirm that? Can you confirm that you characterised it then or understood it to be criminal behaviour, this abuse of prisoners for those purposes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: During an exchange of bodies, the Presidency side were required to exchange two particular bodies. In the instant to which I believe you refer, the individuals had been buried for a period of time. They were brought to the PTT building, where I controlled the body exchange. During the course of that body exchange, prisoners were used to move the bodies of -- that were being returned to the Serb side. I did watch the event. I made observations and objections to it to those on the Presidency side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree, and you did speak about that in your amalgamated statement in paragraph 122 and then paragraph 128 and then when you testified in the Galic case on the 3rd of July, 2002, on page 11.109, that the Muslims, the Muslim Army, often abused civilian locations in order to place their own artillery pieces there? This also pertains to the Kosevo Hospital. It's in your amalgamated statement, paragraph 123, and also in your statement from 1997, on page 12. That's what you say. The purpose of that was to attract Serb fire in order to have the Serbs accused. And then in your reports from October and December 1992, you confirmed that your observers inspected the damage in two hospitals, and you said that you were not satisfied with that kind of behaviour, when artillery pieces, armoured vehicles, et cetera, are being placed within the zone of a hospital. And you say that that is something that did, indeed, occur; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have -- I believe that the Prosecutor already had this as an associated exhibit. 10864 is the 65 ter number, and then let's have 10865 just to gain further insight. Actually, have these documents already been admitted as P documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Since we've received confirmation, we don't need to call up those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with that? Also, do you agree that in your amalgamated statement, in paragraphs 125 and 126, you confirmed that the hospital was often hit by return fire, as it were? Now, there is something I'd like to clarify with you: [In English] "... rather than a military response, because the mobile mortar was gone soon after it fired." [Interpretation] Do you agree that the side that is responding, in this case the Serb side, does not necessarily have to know that the mobile mortar had left; so from that point of view that could have been military response rather than retaliation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one side in a conflict perceives that they need to respond to a military action such as the engagement of, let's take, for example, mortars from a particular location. If, in response to that, you apply force which is in extreme excess to what would be required to destroy the target, if the fall of shot is such that it is so general that you've taken into account the source of the fire against you to very little effect, those would be the reasons I would perceive that there was often an over-reaction, and the time lapse between the initial contact and the response was such that the possibility of the originating units being in the same place were not high. As a commander, I would probably temper my response for a number of reasons. They would be: Saving ammunition, unnecessary collateral damage. Because unless you're trying to destroy the enemy, you'd be really on a pointless mission responding with fire. So it is these balances which we were able to watch and make judgements on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you believe that abuse of civilian locations for these purposes constitutes a crime?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that particular tactic was used within Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, you confirmed in your amalgamated statement, and afterwards in the November and December reports that have already been admitted as Prosecution exhibits, that the Muslim army abused the proximity of the UN forces in order to act against the Serb side and attract Serb fire as a response vis-à-vis these UN installations. Also, you confirmed, in paragraph 68 of your amalgamated statement, that sometimes they would even intentionally target a building using tanks, and it was only the Muslims that had tanks in that area. Do you agree that on several occasions you and other representatives of UNPROFOR asked the Muslim side to move their artillery pieces at least 500 metres away from UN installations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had personal experience of the situations you describe, and we did, on numerous occasions, ask the Presidency side, should they wish to engage the Serb side, if they would be kind enough to do it further away from the UN installations. Yes, I had personal experience of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Mr. Henneberry's diary, on page 1060853, he said: [In English] "That firing on PTT building came from Papa 4 position." [Interpretation] Do you agree with this conclusion? It is in Mr. Henneberry's statement -- or, rather, diary. And in the December 1992 report, this is a report that was tendered by the Prosecution, it says that on the 18th of December, 1992, fire was opened at a vehicle that belonged to the observers, mortar fire, and, therefore, there was a traffic accident and that the Serb driver had also been hit. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall the incident, but I have to make some fairly significant corrections here. If one looks at the map, Papa 4 is located in such a position as I don't believe it could see the PTT building or its surroundings. The officer whose diary you quote from was on Lima side. He was, therefore, on Serb side, outside the city. So where he assumed the information you've read to me, I have no idea. There is also, from what I recall, no record from Papa 4, who would have certainly known of outgoing rounds, saying that those rounds were aimed at or impacted anywhere near the PTT. So I can't accept the statements made by that officer in his diary or his submissions as being truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But what is contained in your December reports, your reports from December 1992, and that is recorded in Henneberry's diary on page 01062856 in relation to the targeting of the observers' vehicle, which led to a traffic accident involving a Serbian vehicle; you confirm that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If we can just be clear for the record here. I think we're talking about two separate incidents. Colonel Mole was responding to the first one, and now Dr. Karadzic is asking about the second. If that distinction can be made clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayden. With that caveat, can you answer the question, Colonel Mole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think I've answered the question relating to the outgoing round from the Papa 4 location. If a traffic accident occurs by virtue of a close impact to a vehicle, I would put it to you nobody would know the origin of the rounds concerned. Certainly, if you were in the vehicle, that's unlikely to be your major interest. You've got to assume, therefore, that somebody was watching that particular incident, as opposed to any other. I've tried to explain the military activity, and impacts that went on on a daily basis were such that to focus on one incident, such as this, and attempt to determine the source of a round, if I can invite you to imagine what it was like within the circumstances we're trying to describe, would be completely irrelevant and impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, that vehicle of yours was on the Serb side. I think it was in Nedzarici. And your report for December 1992 suggests that the fire came from the Muslim side, because Serbs did not shell Serb neighbourhoods; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Colonel, I'd like to come back a little to clarify a point for me, for the Tribunal. You've talked about seeing mortars being used by the Presidency side, mobile mortars. Were there any embedded fixed-plate positions that were being used, to your knowledge, where mortars were fired from on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That tended not to be the case, because if I might take you back to the airport agreement, if any mortars were used on fixed locations, depending on their size, of course, but fixed locations would indicate they would be the larger-calibre mortars, then clearly they would have been included within the airport agreement and we would have monitored those weapons. So in answer to your question, I don't have any personal recollection of the situation you describe, and the mortar attacks I was aware of tend to be smaller calibre and more mobile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And as a supplementary question: Did you observe any long-barrelled artillery? I'm not talking about tanks. I'm talking about either self-propelled guns or long-barrelled artillery weapons being used by the Presidency side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had personal experience of anti-aircraft weapons being used in the direct-fire mode. My understanding was that the heavy weapons, although they're monitored, of course, as they were on the Serb side, didn't prevent their use. It meant that we monitored them. We knew where they were, and they should have remained within a geographical area. That's not quite the way it worked out. It ended up that we, as monitors, watched the war with more convenience by virtue of collections of weapons, which made the job easier for the UNMOs, but it didn't cause the weapons to be taken out of the engagement. I think there is a common misconception that because weapons were monitored they were not engaged in the warfare. That is not the case, as we know from the Serb side. So exactly the same applied on the Presidency side as well. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, it does, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for these clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement of 1997, on pages 11 and 12, you say that you observed the following on Mount Igman: one APC, two Howitzers, two 122-millimetre Howitzers, four 105-millimetre guns, and six 120-millimetre mortars. Do you remember that all of this equipment was used from Mount Igman and that every Serb-held part of Sarajevo could be targeted from Mount Igman, broadly speaking?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may answer the last question first. Yes, the weapons on Mount Igman could have direct effect on any of the units around Sarajevo. The exact composition of the Presidency forces on Mount Igman was an assessment at any one time. Amongst the UNMOs, we had some very experienced artillery officers, and they were able to make those assessments. But it would be a mistake to specify exactly what was on Igman at any one time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have 15 minutes to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With the assistance and the courtesy of Colonel Mole, if I manage to ask questions that can be answered with a yes or no, I will perhaps make it. But it will be a pity if this witness goes away without giving us a full picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said in your amalgamated statement that the Muslims had two T-54 tanks, they had also anti-aircraft weapons that they used as direct-fire weapons, and again in the Galic case, on the 3rd of July, 2002, on page 11097, you also testified that the Muslims shelled the airport from Butmir. Can you confirm that here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't the statement in front of me. But if that's what the statement says, I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then in your amalgamated statement, paragraph 104, you confirmed that on the 26th November, 1992, you reported that the Muslims used mortars to shell the transformer station in Blazuj, resulting in an interruption of the water supply, which was their response to the fact that the Serbs cut off the water supply to Hrasnica. Do you agree that that transformer station and the availability of electricity was crucial to the water supply for Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arranged utility missions - you'll forgive me, but I'm not an electrician, and I took, as read, what the utility missions were there to achieve from the engineers within UNPROFOR, within the sector headquarters, so I can't pass comment about what the transformer station provided in the way of power to whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is in your amalgamated statement, paragraph 104. If you remember Bacevo, the main source of water supply was on the Serb side, and it was receiving electricity from the transformer station. And if the Muslims targeted and hit that particular transformer station, then the water supply would be cut off. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's in the statement, then that's as I stand by it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your amalgamated statement, paragraphs 131 and 132, you said the Muslims took advantage of Sarajevo's situation to elicit sympathy, and for that purpose they restricted the movement of civilians and they kept their population in Sarajevo for that purpose. That's in those two paragraphs. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have those two paragraphs in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that at the time when you were there, there were about 60.000 Serbs in a part of Sarajevo controlled by the Muslims, and that we, through General Morillon, through public appeals, tried to ensure the freedom of movement of civilians and give them the right to move to a territory where they would feel safer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within Sarajevo, there was a considerable ethnic mix. The numerics I can't recall, unless I stated them in previous dispositions. But, yes, there were a considerable number of Serbs within Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In certain passages, you confirmed that the 1st Corps was in Sarajevo, that out of the 70.000 members of the 1st Corps approximately a half were within the inner city. You confirmed that you had heard of Juka Prazina and other criminals who had their own brigades. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that all these things put together, provoking fire from the other side, the media pressure on the Serbs, the biased attitude of the reporters and even some politicians who were effectively anti-Serb, all these things removed us further and further away from peace? Can you name today a politician whose attitude, whose position, really grated on your ears?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a soldier and even as a retired soldier, I'm not very comfortable about answering that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We can do without. But I do want to note that you, yourself, noted such things. You said in your statement --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get 1D2227.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that there were clear indications -- [In English] " ... clear indications that there is not a well-co-ordinated and unified command structure on either side." [Interpretation] It's 1D2227. We discussed it a little yesterday. Do you agree that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had inherited territorial and municipal armies that were already in existence, and everyone, from General Sipcic to General Milosevic, had great problems establishing a unified command structure over these local units?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly a significant difficulty which I observed that both sides had. This was not a unique experience from the Serb side. So I understand what you're saying. I was sympathetic to that situation, and I agree with your overall assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless it has been admitted so far, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D540, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now call up 65 ter 11575.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is from the time of General Sipcic -- no, it was already General Galic. Colonel Marcetic writes here that local leaders and their supporters are out of control in certain areas, and these difficulties are encountered all the time, starting with Sipcic who found the worst situation because it was early days, the VRS had just been set up. But even in November the corps command is encountering the same problem. Is this consistent with what you confirmed earlier?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I've never seen the document, obviously, but it's fully in accord with what we understood to be the case. So, yes, I understand your point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why do we have only a partial translation of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the translation from the Galic case. We did not have our own resources to translate the entire document ourselves, but we don't mind if a translation is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If, Mr. Hayden, you are happy with this translation, we'll admit it. Otherwise, we can put it being marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If it can be marked for identification. We'll get back to you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll mark it for identification, pending full translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D541, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in these circumstances, when the Serb side was under pressure from many sides in many ways and a complete lack of a single command, is it implied that firing rounds or even shells did not necessarily mean that the Serb authorities, starting from higher commands, ordered or instigated certain incidents? Do you agree that it would be quite unreasonable, incomprehensible, and implausible that the Serb side, with all its trained officers that it had, should go on shooting in its own foot day after day?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is definitely a question which does not get answered by a yes or a no. You state that the Serb side had a complete lack of a single command. Nothing could be further from the truth. Any military formation which can bring a fire mission down on a concentrated area, such as Otes, from a disparate group, geographically spread of heavy weapons, throughout the city cannot possibly portray a lack of single command. Therefore, if you remove that part of the comment from your statement, the rest of what you said there I can't agree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree with you as far as operations are concerned, but perhaps I wasn't clear enough. I meant to ask about incidents. You intervened in certain incidents, and the higher command redressed the situation immediately in every case. But concerning shooting, do you agree that there were altogether too many weapons in Bosnia in private hands, it was available for purchase, and just before the war and during the war huge amounts of weapons were stolen? I'm talking about privately-owned weapons, I'm talking about poor control by local units, regarding incidents, not regarding well-planned operations. Do you agree that there is a distinction?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two parts to answer there. There was a war. A war is a continuum. The incidents all joined up. They were not divisible so that you could suggest that that particular incident was caused by a certain set of events. It isn't that straightforward. I can't explain to you, if you're not a soldier and you haven't been engaged in such activities, any clearer than I have tried to, that this was not a controlled situation; this was a war in progress. The incidents all joined together. They were not divisible. You could not apply blame to one as opposed to another, nor was the ability of the UN to attempt to explain, as you are trying to explain, the difficulties which were experienced by the combatants. As for your comment about privately-owned weapons, yes, of course there were, but let's be totally clear. There were not privately-owned heavy weapons. All the heavy weapons around Sarajevo that we either saw or monitored were not owned by individuals. They were part of the structure of the Serb forces around Sarajevo. But your point about the difficulty of command and control, as opposed to the attempt at command and control, is a good one. There were geographical difficulties. There were structural difficulties. There were personality conflicts. There was history which you have alluded to by suggesting that certain areas had been defended by local people who had then become absorbed within the Serb military structure. I hope I've explained it the way you would like it to be explained in that regard. So we were fully conversant with the difficulties and the structure, but I do have to correct you on the items that I started my response with there that relates to the command and control and private weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your last question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How about two, Your Excellencies? I just wanted to ask the colonel:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have insight into this UK Military Manual, Colonel, and do you agree that this is something that every army should have, every army should follow such rules?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the interview we had with the colonel, we gave him excerpts from the military manual of the UK that we will use later in this trial, and these experts explain these terms; military targets, sniping, legitimate targets, et cetera. I just wanted to ask the colonel if he is familiar with this manual and if it forms a basic set of regulations for the conduct of the UK army. And then I'll ask my next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I clarify the document you're speaking of? Is that Rules of Conflict, or Manual of Military Law, or what would that be? I've read a lot of books when I did staff jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is Chapter 5 of the UK Military Manual that we have given you, if you remember. In fact, we gave you some excerpts from the UK Military Manual. Do you agree that this is a basic set of rules for any army to follow, a good basis for any army to follow?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, now I understand the book to which you refer. Yes, the one we discussed I have had sight of, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 25, line 5 -- in fact, it's page 24. Page 24, line 5. There seems to be an error in the transcript. I think you said in your answer, "I can agree," and it's recorded as "I can't agree."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could that please be corrected in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And my last question: In your 1997 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think Colonel Mole is able to scroll back the transcript. I heard that with care, but I'm confident the colonel said, "I can't agree." If I can tell you, it's a question about -- that you answered with: "Nothing could be further from the truth," as regards the complete lack of a single command. At the end of your answer, did you say or not: "Therefore, if you remove that part of the comment from your statement, the rest of what you said there I can't agree with"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I meant, sir, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that if we removed that part of the comment, you can agree with the rest. But it must be the language barrier that we have between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, in your statement from 1997, on page 14, you said that you had never had the feeling that Karadzic or Mladic had a direct involvement in day-to-day events in Sarajevo: [In English] "... day-to-day events in Sarajevo." [Interpretation] That we never had a direct hand in the daily events in Sarajevo, in view of all our work, contacts with foreigners, travel, et cetera. Is that was said in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it makes perfect sense. That's why General Galic commanded the corps, and that's why you did the job you did. Of course, the impact from outside that General Galic responded to would have been political pressure and, from General Mladic, presumably, military pressure or direction as determined by others above him. But, quite right, on a day-to-day basis, that was the task of the Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, I think you can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: We have time before the break, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or if you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: It won't be longer than five minutes, under ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed and have a break afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Colonel Mole, this morning we spoke about the testimony -- observations of Captain Patrick Henneberry. You noted at transcript page 15 that he, at least at the 8th of December, was working on the Lima side or the Bosnian Serb side. During your tour, did he ever work on the Papa side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And why was that the case? Why can you be sure that if he worked on the Lima side on the 8th of December, he never worked on the Papa side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I explained before, that when you were, as a UN military observer, designated to go to Sarajevo, the last time that you saw the people with whom you arrived in Sarajevo, if they were on the other side, was as you left the overall briefing in the PTT building. And then once you went to Lima side or once you stayed within the city, that was where your tour of duty continued until its completion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Would Captain Henneberry or officers on the Lima side be involved in investigations conducted on the Papa side by UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And would they be privy to official communication emanating from the Papa side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is one rider to my answer of no, in that we had an open radio network, so everybody could hear what was going on from one side to the other. But remember that the open radio network was one that responded and was used for everyday physical activity, as opposed to policy or any other decision. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. If an observation post observed a -- for example, Muslim fire onto the PTT building in the city, for example, would that have been recorded in the daily situation report that you authored?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Colonel, at paragraph 39 of your amalgamated statement, you discuss the weaponry that you observed the Presidency to have on the Papa side. Yesterday, we were -- you were describing the widely-dispersed or heavy bombardment of the city. To your knowledge, was the weaponry described in paragraph 39 capable of being responsible for such widely-dispersed attacks on the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the only equipment within range of the city that could perform the sorts of fire missions and other high-explosive events that occurred within the city belonged to those outside the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If I can ask Mr. Registrar for D537.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Colonel Mole, this is the map that you marked yesterday in cross-examination at the request of Dr. Karadzic. And do you recall marking "3" where Ilidza was, or the Serb part of Ilidza was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, at transcript page 5833, Dr. Karadzic drew your attention to paragraph 84 of your statement, where you discuss the Otes offensive, and you state that: "In addition to the Otes offensive, shells were landing elsewhere in the city." And then two pages on at T-5835, Dr. Karadzic discussed the contents of a newspaper article with you from AFP, and that was tendered as Exhibit D535. And if I can just refresh your memory as to the portion of that article he drew your attention to. It stated that: "Tuesday's fighting around the airport started when Bosnian infantry units attacked Serbian forces stationed in the village of Ilidza, which borders the airport. The Serbs responded with intense artillery fire that shook the entire sector. Commander Barry Frewer, a spokesman for the UN troops in Sarajevo, said Wednesday." Dr. Karadzic asked you if you knew who Commander Frewer was, and then said to you: "Would you agree that in parallel with the fighting for Otes and Zuc, there was fighting in other parts of the city as well?" And you said you noticed no variation in what we would perceive as the normal front-line activities elsewhere. Now, Colonel Mole, accepting that what was reported in the article was true, that is, that there was fighting occurring in Ilidza that was started by a Bosnian offensive, would that account for or explain the shells that you say in your statement were, quote, "landing elsewhere in the city"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your objection, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that would be speculation. It would be a leading question, rather, and speculation as well. The witness cannot speculate about intentions and the origins of that fire, and he cannot tie it to this, although Colonel Mole had said that war is an entity. So we're not only talking about Sarajevo, but the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But I think this question is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with you, Mr. Karadzic. It's triggered from your question, and it does not call for Colonel Mole's speculation. Did you conclude your question, or are you able to answer the question, Mr. Mole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I think so, yes. Could I go back to the map, please? Would that be acceptable?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: That was D537.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. If one considers the location marked to, which was the target of the Serb forces to take away what they considered a considerable threat in the area of Otes -- and may I mark that map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you can mark it separately, and we can keep it separate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we can use a blue colour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm colour-blind, so ... If I mark the map in that line there [marks], from my understanding, the intentions of the Serb side was to remove the Presidency side in the area marked "2," that enclave, back to that particular line, which would allow them, as you can see from the map, a geographical line from the airport area or Ilidza or "3" up the road to where I've just marked in blue and around to - I'll continue with my blue - around here [marks]. Besides the obvious problem that the Serbs perceived they had in Otes as a threat to Ilidza, that was also a significant, sort of, tactical objective. So, now, to come back to the question. It's important, I think, that any action that occurred in that zone of "2" would have immediate repercussion within the immediate area, so any attack, say, from Butmir to Ilidza, or from anywhere else on Ilidza, would be an understandable response to what went on in the area of Otes. What I'm referring to in the answer to Dr. Karadzic's question as to the level of activity elsewhere in the city, and which I believe you're asking, I am considering elsewhere beyond to the east of those areas that I've marked out. Therefore, the front-line which circulates -- goes completely around Sarajevo, there was a little increase in tension, of course, but there was considerable incoming high-explosive rounds into the city which we saw no connection with the events that I've just tried to describe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. If you could kindly put your signature and date again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit this map again. This will be a new P exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1436, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Judge Morrison has some further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Just one thing, Colonel Mole. The radio net that was common to Papa and Lima positions, was that encrypted or was that an open?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an open net, sir, available to everybody. Indeed, so open that we gave hand-sets on the same frequency to Serb liaison officers with us in the PTT and to Presidency liaison officers available to us as well, the intention being to show that our activities were completely open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your evidence has been concluded. Thank you very much for your coming to The Hague to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will have a break for a bit more than 20 minutes. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Gaynor and Dr. Subotic. I take it the next witness is Mr. Higgs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As for the time for cross-examination, the Trial Chamber advised the parties yesterday that Mr. Karadzic would have three hours for his cross-examination of Mr. Higgs. The Chamber's determination that three hours is a reasonable time for cross-examination of Mr. Higgs was made on the basis of the criteria that we have previously set out, and particularly in light of the fact that Mr. Higgs's evidence is of a limited nature. He did not conduct the original investigation into the various shelling incidents discussed in his expert report, but, rather, provides analysis and his own conclusions based upon his review of those reports and observation that he made substantially after the incidents in question. The Chamber considers that three hours is ample time for the accused to cross-examine him on his methodology in reviewing the original investigations and in reaching his conclusions and to challenge him on those conclusions. However, as we have previously stated, should the accused demonstrate, in the course of his cross-examination, that additional time is warranted, the Chamber will consider the matter further. Unless there's other procedural matters, we'll bring in the witness. Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, there is one procedural matter on which the Defence and Prosecution have reached agreement, and that concerns part of the report of Mr. Higgs which concerns Incident G-16, which appears on page 12 of the report and goes on --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the Defence were going to make a motion for the exclusion of that part of the report. Our position is that we agree that that part of the report need not be admitted in evidence as part of the evidence of Mr. Higgs. However, we do wish to preserve the position which we set out in our submission of the 31st of August, 2009, and which we repeated in the notification which accompanied the marked-up indictment in this case, that it will be in the interests of justice in certain instances, in our submission, that the Trial Chamber should hear evidence on incidents which have been removed from the indictment pursuant to Rule 73 bis. And we'll be relying, among other things, on the Appeals Chamber's decision in the Seselj case on the 9th of January, 2008. So I won't say anything more about that at the moment. We do wish to reserve our position in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. In any event, those parts which will not be admitted into evidence will be redacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We haven't yet taken that step, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we'll take that step.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for the agreement. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Higgs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could kindly take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you state your full name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Mr. Richard James Higgs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You are of British nationality?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You served in the British Army for 22 years, from 1980 to 2002; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just taking you to the position from 1987 to 2002, could you give the Court a general overview of what the nature of your duties was during that period?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: From 1987 onwards, I worked specifically with mortars. I started with working within a training establishment, teaching mortars, various levels of degrees of expertise, to soldiers in the British Army and also to international students, teaching the operational deployment, technical information, tactical information, and ballistic knowledge at that time. I then moved into a advisory role with our forces based in Germany, where I was responsible for all their training, advising again on all technical, tactical, and ballistical information, and assisting them should there be any safety-type incidents or anything that needed investigating with mortars. I would then manage that on their behalf, advise them accordingly to make sure everything was done correctly, to find out if anything happened, why it happened, and so on. I then moved into a similar role, but this time working globally, advising not only British Army but foreign armies on the use of, again, mortars operationally and their technical and ballistic capabilities, and also moving into the development of mortars. And then my final role was as the divisional instructor for the British Army, which is the subject-matter expert of mortars on behalf of the whole British Army. So I was seen as the technical expert on mortars. And within that role I advised the British Army, again, during all their training, operational and tactical requirements, but I led on the ballistical safety information which I, again, taught, and my responsibilities were to ensure that all firings were carried out safely and in accordance, of course, with methodologies. And I also advised, during this time, various overseas countries in the same areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you've, no doubt, attended a great number of live-firing exercises. Could you just give the Court an overall view of the number of live-firing exercises you've attended?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Difficult to give an exact number. But during the period especially where I was delivering training, we would be live firing sometimes three to four times a week, for weeks on end. And during my advisory role when I was based in Germany, again, I would be sometimes visiting live firing probably, again, three to four days a week, with hundreds if not thousands of rounds being fired on each of those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Similarly, could you give the Court an overall picture of the number of crater analysis exercises you would have participated in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: During the training part of my activities, we teach one part which is identification of a direction of what's called hostile battery, which is where the rounds may be seen to be coming from. As part of that, I have probably looked at many hundreds of different craters, as part of that training. As far as investigations are concerned where an incident has occurred, again, difficult to give precise numbers, but many tens if not into the hundreds, even, of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your report, you've referred to, on a number of instances, to the concept of prerecorded targets. I would just like you to explain briefly how you understand prerecording of targets works in an extended siege situation of a specific town or city.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: To make the firing of mortars more accurate, to save them having to waste time and ammunition with trying to adjust or move the rounds onto the target, it will save time if the targets are what is known as prerecorded. This can be done in a number of ways. But by prerecording a target, the mortar position will know the correct bearing, elevation, and information they put on a mortar to hit that target with a higher degree of accuracy the first time. The longer you are in a position, so if mortars are in a position for extended periods of time, they can build up lists of prerecorded targets over a wide area, which will then mean that if they have to engage a target anywhere within that area, they will have a higher degree of hitting that target without first adjusting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You've previously testified at the Tribunal in -- at this Tribunal in the trial of Dragomir Milosevic and the trial of Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And you have prepared a consolidated report containing information relevant to incidents which are relevant to this particular case; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 11144, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On the screen in front of you, you see a document. Is that the report which you've prepared for this case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And you've had the opportunity to review that report over the past few days?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you wish to make any corrections or amendments to it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And do you adopt it as part of your evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender the report at this stage for admission, subject to the redaction of the part of the report concerning G-16, as indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1437, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I propose to take the witness to 12 documents and 1 video, which are only some of the documents referred to in this report. And I'd like 65 ter 18178 to be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Higgs, at page -- I'll move on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I have document 11378, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Higgs, on the left-hand side of the screen in front of you, you see a document which is addressed to HQ UNPROFOR, Zagreb, and which is -- could you confirm that this is the document referred to in your report concerning an incident which took place on the 12th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if we just go to the third page of that document, as you can see, on the last paragraph on the left-hand side of your screen, you see the words: "This shell could have been shot from corridor Nedzarici-Ilidza Nord." You can see those words?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, do you have any observations to make about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: From this particular incident, from the evidence I've seen, from the incident reports, including this one, the way in which the round landed, it was not possible to come up with a definite range or even a confirmed direction. So both the reports, as best as possible with the information they had, came up using the information gathered at the scene with an approximate direction from which the rounds came, and that is the area stated there in that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like document 11394 to be brought up. I'm informed this is an alternative number for the document we were trying to look at a moment ago. That document, in fact, we'll come to later, if that's -- sorry. Sorry, we'll -- if we could move to the third page of that document in the English language. There should be an English translation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, we see the reference in that document. Do you -- can you confirm that that is a document which you used in compiling your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, on the left-hand side, it's quite difficult to see, but you can see, towards the end of the document, the words: "The ballistic expert found remnants of an artillery shell, most probably an 82-millimetre mortar shell; most probably fired from direction Nedzarici." Do you have any observations about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Again, because of the poor, if you like, data at the scene, because this round impacted within a person, all they could do was confirm the calibre of the weapon, in this case an 80-millimetre, and an approximate direction. And the direction stated in this document is the same as the one we saw in the previous document, that area of Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to the next document, which is 15051. This concerns Incident G-6.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your report on Incident G-6, Mr. Higgs, you refer to some differences in the reports you've seen concerning this incident, and I'd just like to explore those with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could go to the second page of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You see that this is a compilation of a number of different documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in the second-last paragraph, towards the end, we see the words: "Type of destruction of the explosion site indicates that the shell was an 82-millimetre mortar shell, fired from the west, where the enemy position is located at the Institute for the Blind at Nedzarici. Shell stabiliser was not found at the explosion site." And on the following page, the third paragraph down, we see the words -- again, a reference: "The type of destruction at the explosion site indicates that the shell was an 82-millimetre shell, fired from the west, where the enemy position is located at the Institute for the Blind at Nedzarici. A 120-millimetre shell stabiliser was found near the explosion site." Do you provide any observations about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Obviously, this is from the initial investigation from the scene which these -- this team attended first. They ascertained from the damage and the materials at that scene that the 82-millimetre rounds were the rounds that landed in the street and that the tail-fin, from their examination, was not part or had anything to do with those two rounds, as they concluded it fell sometime earlier. And this report also alludes to the firing of a 120-millimetre round which landed in a different location, where no casualties were caused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next document, please, which is 19725. Can you see the first pages of this are the French original, and on the fifth page the English translation exists? If we could move to the fifth page of this document, please. Go on to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise this document, Mr. Higgs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: This is the consolidated report from -- that was produced by the French officer, Verdy, the day after the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if we can move a little further down the screen there, we see the words: "In my estimation, the strikes were probably launched from a zone under the control of the Bosnian Serbs." Do you have any reason to -- did you have any observations about that sentence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: To come up to this estimation from the reports, they're using, obviously, the estimated direction, which is from the west, which puts it into that area of Nedzarici, which is under the control of the Bosnian Serbs. So that is where they're getting this estimation from.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to disagree with that assertion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: From the evidence seen in both reports, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if we could move to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, under item E, the report states: "Type of ammunition: Mortar, 120 millimetres." And under D it says that there were three hits. Do you have any comment about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: This is where, as I mentioned in my report, it differs from the initial forensic examination, as they came to the conclusion of one 120-millimetre and two 82-millimetre. The problem that Captain Verdy has is this investigation was carried out a day later and he was not available to have all the evidence of the investigation team who carried out the investigation on the day. That is probably the reason why he has assumed they were all 120 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Which of the two reports do you think is more accurate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I would have a tendency to believe the report that was conducted on the day, as the best way of conducting any incident of this manner is as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: All right. Can I have document 09623, please. We're moving on to a different incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the number again?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The number is 09623.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: As we'll see in a moment, this concerns the shelling of the Markale Market-Place which took place on the 5th of February, 1994, sometimes referred to as "Markale I." Now, once again, is this one of the documents you used in compiling your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could take the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, as you can see from the third paragraph, Mr. Higgs -- sorry, the last paragraph on that page, there is a reference to "the transverse axis of the ellipse was north-north-east." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: When they were looking at the shape of the crater on the ground, they could see that it was pointing towards that north-north-east direction. And later in the report, they actually measured that and came up with an angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We can move to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, at the end of the first paragraph on that page, we see the words stating: "It was an 18-degree angle from north to east, with a plus or minus 5-degree tolerance added to the angle difference value." Can you explain what that is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes. Having had a look at the shape of the crater on the ground, they have then conducted their examination and calculated that the direction from the point of ground where the round hit, from whence the round came, is a bearing of 18 degrees, obviously plus or five [sic] the 5-degrees tolerance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the report makes a conclusion that this was what kind of projectile?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: It was a 120-millimetre projectile, which in this case could be proven because the tail-fins of the round were still in the crater and could be used for investigation purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Does this report make any conclusions concerning the range, which is to say the distance the projectile travelled?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If I could move to the next document, please, which is 09630.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your expert report, Mr. Higgs, you've said that the UNPROFOR report at Reference B just goes back up the report -- just - I beg your pardon - just goes to back up the report at Reference A with the same findings. There's only one piece of information that does not tie up - this is some of the points made by Captain Verdy - but these are rectified further on in the report. And I want to ask you a few questions to explore that point. Now, on the page in front of you, what do you see there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: This is a part of the report from Captain Verdy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I want to move to page 8 of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could go on. This is a cover fax. And on the next page we see a document headed "UNPROFOR Investigation Report, Sarajevo Market Explosion of 5th of February, 1994." This is the report which you examined in compiling your own report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And if we could move to not the next page, but two pages on. At the bottom of paragraph 17 it says: "There is insufficient physical evidence to prove that one party or the other fired the mortar bomb. The mortar bomb in question could have been fired by either side." Do you have any comments about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: When they carried -- conducted the crater examination, they were able to conduct the bearing from which the round came, and they were able to determine an approximate angle at which the round hit the ground.
