The problem we have with mortars is that they have a number-charged system, and all the charges could deliver that same angle when the round hits the ground, so, therefore, it gives you a large parameter, from a reasonably close range up to the maximum range, where the round could have been fired from. That is the reason why they put that statement in, because at the time that this report was produced, that's as much as they could confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to move to another part of this report, which is another nine pages on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You see the reference under Conclusion C. It says that: "The bomb impacted, having approached at a bearing of between 0330 and 0420 mils," and then three letters which are not legible. Do you have any observations about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: This particular incident was investigated by many teams. I think 10 teams, in total, produced reports. The forensic team used degrees, and as we have already mentioned, they came to a bearing of 18 degrees. Eighteen degrees is approximately 320 mils, so you can see that it aligns with many of these other reports where they get a bearing between about 0320 and 0420.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to go to a table which is on five pages previously to this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We can see, under part 2, it says there were a total of 10 crater analyses conducted on the crater.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And if we could look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, see the paragraph marked "Bearing." In the final part of that paragraph, it says -- it's referring here to Captain Verdy: "However, based on his note, he appears to have made a mathematical error which led to an incorrect final back-bearing. Therefore, although his method may have been sound, based on the figures he used, his results were flawed." Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes. There were 10 examinations carried out, but for some reason the one that Captain Verdy did came up with different information. Obviously, the investigating team at the time have looked at that and have decided that he must have made some form of mathematical error to come up with information completely different to the other eight reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: All right. If you could look at the table of results and just explain briefly to the Court what your analysis of that table is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: You can see there the list of all the 10 sets of information that were taken from the various investigations taking place. The top two, or the two that were -- have been kind of questioned in the report, that we've just seen with the French team with Captain Verdy, have come up with different information. The other eight, from Major Russell down to the bottom, you can see that their results are all very similar in their findings, and those results also agree with the 18 degrees found by the investigation -- the CSB investigation team.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: For the record, could you tell us what 18 degrees is approximately equivalent to in the mils measurement system?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: It's approximately 320 mils.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So the report conducted by the Bosnian authorities is consistent with eight of the results in front of you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to 11333, please. I'm moving on to another incident. This is the incident known as Markale II.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your report, under Incident G-19, Mr. Higgs, you have relied on a considerable number of documents in your analysis concerning this incident. I just want you to confirm that the documents, as they come up, are the documents which you relied upon. Now, the document in front of you is obviously an UNMO daily sitrep.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to go to page 20 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: As we see towards the end of the document - if we could scroll down a little bit - this is a description of an incident which took place at the market-place and includes the words: "One projectile was fired from 170 mag deg, killed 33 TBC people (UNMO confirmed 31 killed) and wounded 79." Focusing on that sentence, what are your comments?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: This is relating to the round that fell in the road, and it's just confirming that the bearing from which, again, was measured on the day for the direction at which the round came from was 170 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On the next page, at the top, we see in the second paragraph the words: "Two of the remaining four impacts caused 07 injuries (not confirmed). These four rounds were fired from a different bearing (220 to 240 mag deg) and impacted 300 metres further south from the above projectile." This is an issue which you've referred to in your report. Could you explain what those words mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Obviously, the same day as the previous round or the previous incident happened, there were four other impacts from 120-millimetre mortar, as referred to here, which landed at approximately 300 metres away, and their investigation found that the direction of those was 220 to 240. At this moment in time, they're being seen as separate incidents. But as the investigation proceeded, many assumptions were made that these were part of the same firing, and that's what led to some confusion and assumptions being made in some of the future information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And is it correct that from this sitrep the fatal round is recorded as coming from 170 degrees?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could move now to 09917.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, on the left-hand part of the screen in front of you, Mr. Higgs, you can see, from the first paragraph, that this is a cover sheet to which is attached the final and comprehensive report on the Sarajevo mortar incident of 28th August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could move now to two pages further on. In fact, we can move to the next page, please. And if we could scroll slightly to the left at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The report refers to "Key Evidence," and then on the next page, please, we see what that key evidence is, in summary -- what the key evidence is, in summary, followed by a summary of this report. So I'd just like to you explain to Their Honours in a little bit of detail the criteria which you would take into account in determining the origin of fire of the fatal projectile. So if we can start with the first point, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, it talks us through the impact analysis. There, it confirms the fine-point investigations. The French engineer report came to 2850 mils, which, again, converted into degrees is approximately 170, and that the UNMO report -- the initial UNMO report also got 170 degrees. It also then confirms that the other four impacts produced bearings of 220 to 240 degrees. It then starts to make assumptions with the next sentence, where it says: "The follow-on investigation sought to clarify this apparent discrepancy." So somebody thought at this stage that the rounds were connected, even though they landed 300 metres apart, which, for mortars firing in this scenario, is a huge distance apart. This assumption, then, did affect some of their thinking, as you'll see a bit later on. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry. If I can stop you on that point. Can you explain why it is not possible, in your view, that the four impacts came from the same location as the fatal impact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: If -- when a mortar engages a target, you have a bearing or a line from that mortar to where the round landed on the ground, which you can then trace back. Because the other round landed 300 metres apart, if you then traced back a line with the same bearing from that point backwards, it would come to a point 300 metres different where the mortar was to the first one. So for the same mortar to have fired both, it would have had to have fired the one of the four rounds, then in very quick succession quickly pack up, move 300 metres across to one side, set up again, and then fire the other round to give you the same bearing back to the same mortar position. The other problem which is mentioned in this paragraph, which is the next sentence where it says they have used the fused furrow for calculating the bearing, using correct mortar methodologies for investigation, you do not use fused furrows for calculating bearing because they are prone to error. An experienced investigator would not use a fused furrow unless the fuse furrow was of excellent quality. And I mention what that is in, I believe, para 10 of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, do you discount the possibility of a ricochet by the fatal projectile, which is alluded to in the final sentence of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: There is no evidence I have seen to confirm that a round has struck a building first. If it did, it could well have exploded on impact. If they believe that a round had struck a building first and moved it bearing-wise away from where it has come from, then it does not make sense why you would then use the crater fuse-furrow examination to work out the back-bearing, knowing that it's hit a building first. So, no, I don't believe that this round hit a building first. There's no evidence to prove that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You're familiar with the Cymbeline radar system?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain briefly what it is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The Cymbeline is a mortar-locating radar. It projects radar beams into the sky which can then pick up projectiles passing through those radar beams to determine where the round has been fired from.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, just looking at the report, had this fatal projectile been fired at a range of 950 metres or less, what would have happened?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: As you can see from the Cymbeline report, if the mortar had been fired at a very close distance to the incident, then, because of the high trajectory required, the Cymbeline would have detected it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Moving to paragraph 5 on the page in front of you, there is a reference to UN observation posts. I want you to describe to Their Honours why this is relevant, the auditory element.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: From reading this report and others, there was no reported sound of the mortar firing from any of the observer positions. But they did hear the rounds falling, which would indicate that from wherever the mortar was fired, that probably because of something, either buildings or hill-side, were possibly in the way, preventing them hearing the rounds being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your report, at page 33, you have identified four possible ranges from which the projectile could have been fired if it were to approach at an angle of 70 degrees, which we'll get to. The ranges you give are: with a charge 1, 900 metres; with a charge 2, 1600 metres; with a charge 3, 2.400 metres; and with a charge 4, 3.000 metres. In respect of the fatal projectile fired on the market-place, which of those four ranges do you believe to be the most likely, and on what basis do you reach that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: From the evidence received from examining the crater, as we get an angle out of which the round could have coming in at, which then gives us those possible ranges when looking at the range tables, at the close of distance of 900, that would put the mortar inside the confrontation line and also within earshot of the closest UN observer. At 1600 metres, that puts the mortar very close to the confrontation lines and also within earshot of the UN observer. When you go back to charges 3 and 4, it is now placing the mortar beyond the confrontation line, into the hills or surrounding country-side overlooking Sarajevo. Because we heard no sound, and the Cymbeline radar, for the reasons in the report, didn't pick up any angle of the mortar travelling, that would indicate that 900 metres is not the preferred option. At 1600 metres, again, not hearing any sound and because of very poor tactical deployment by putting a mortar right on the confrontation line, would tend to rule out it was fired from 1600 metres. Again because the Cymbeline suggests that it was fired from probably more of a medium charge, those of charges 3 or 4, so it would fire under the radar, and that no sound of the firing was heard, may indicate that the mortar actually was located in the hill-sides overlooking Sarajevo, which would indicate either fired on charges 3 or 4, which would then place it beyond the confrontation line, into Serb-held territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: At this point, could you just explain the concept of charge 1, charge 2, charge 3, charge 4, in the use of a mortar?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The propellant of a mortar can be removed to give you different ranges. They are like plastic wedges or cheeses, as they are called, that go around the tail-fin of a mortar, and most mortars have six of them. And if you only want to fire at close range, you can just put one or two on. If you want to fire at longer ranges, you can put as many as you want on, up to six. But normally with mortars you try and fire at the minimum charge you can to hit the target, because that is more accurate, to fire on the minimum charge; you have less time of flight, and less chances of piece of equipment, like Cymbeline, detecting the round once fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to have to move on, I'm afraid. Could I have document 15059.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This is an UNMO daily sitrep which is referred to in your statement. I'd just like you to confirm that that is the document to which you referred; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the next document, please, which is 15060.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This document -- first, the document is a document from G2 to the commander of UNPROFOR, dated the 8th of September, 1995, concerning the Markale II incident, and it describes in some detail the Cymbeline point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page, please, under point C.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It says that: "A mortar fired from middle to long range would have a lower trajectory and equates to a firing position on Bosnian Serb territory. A lower trajectory round would have been passed under the Cymbeline radar's beam." Do you agree generally with that analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to take you to 15061, please. This is a set of photographs taken following the Markale II incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could go to page 10 when it arrives. In fact, if we could take the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What do you see there, Mr. Higgs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: This is a photograph taken looking down on the mortar crater.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can you just make any comments about the origin of fire and -- yeah, origin of fire, first of all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: From looking at the mortar crater, the experienced eye can see that the majority of the shrapnel marks in the tarmac are between the point of burst on the ground and the pavement, so it gives an indication that this round has come from over the building and that the direction of fire is approximately from where you can see that crater on the ground towards the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How is the angle of impact of the projectile calculated?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: In this case here, none of the investigating teams attending on the first day found a fuse furrow, which is the hole you get in the center of the crater, good enough to use for calculations of angle. Therefore, they conducted a mathematical calculation using measurements measured from the crater to the building and the height of the building to find out what the minimum elevation would have to be to clear the building. And in addition to that, the Bosnian investigation team conducted ballistic calculations on the explosion to give them an approximate angle of decent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What was that angle?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: From the ballistic calculation, they came up with 70 degrees, and the mathematical calculation to the roof gave them a minimum angle of 67 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to take to you the next document, which is 15062. This document is an official report of Sarajevo CSB, dated the 29th of August, 1995. Sorry, could we try 11404, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The document that's coming up, Mr. Higgs, is, I believe, the Sarajevo CSB report which you referred to in --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry, that's not the correct document. Sorry, could I have 11404. I'll move on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, I'd like to take you to 15062. I apologise. On the form, it's 14404.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: My apologies to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, you see this is a CSB Sarajevo report, dated 29th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And further down, it refers to the involvement of a Captain Higgs from Great Britain. That is not, in fact, you, is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, on the next page, please, we see a reference to a 120-millimetre shell, KB 9307, and MK M974. Is it -- you agree that it's possible to take those kind of data from a stabiliser?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, this information was taken from the tail-fins or the stabiliser of the round and can be seen in some of the photographs taken by the investigation teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, under point number 2, it says: "The shell was fired from the south. Its azimuth of 170 degrees, plus or minus 5 degrees, corresponds to aggressor positions at the Trebevic area." Ignoring the reference to aggressor positions, do you have any comment about the 170 degrees?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Now, this is the reading they got from their examination, and I've got no reasons to not believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: There are a couple of diagrams which appear at the very end of this document, four pages from the end. If we could go there, please. We'll leave that document for the moment. Could I ask for Video 40221 to be played, please. I'm informed we need to switch to Sanction for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We could just pause there briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, based on your knowledge of the 120-millimetre mortar system, is the damage we've seen there consistent with a single round?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That comment was made at 1 minute and 25 seconds. If we could play on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if we could pause there, please, pausing at 1 minute and 43 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What is the location depicted in this video?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The video shows an area just outside a building where I'm informed contained within is a market.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How far is this from the open-air market?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: It is a short distance down the road. I have not accurately measured it, but between 50 and 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And the open-air market is where the Markale I projectile exploded; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And this is the location where the Markale II projectile exploded; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could play on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could pause there, please. We're pausing now at 3 minutes and 43 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What do you see in front of you at this point, Mr. Higgs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The video is now showing the arrival of the French investigation team.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you play on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could pause there, please. We're at 4 minutes and 37 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What appears to be taking place at this point in the video?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The team are now taking the measurements from the shell crater to the edge of the building. These measurements are then used when they calculate the height of the building and then work out the minimum angle that the round must have had to clear the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just to clarify your answer there, they're measuring the distance from the crater to the edge of the building, and then what other measurements would they need to take?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: They'll then take the measurement of the height of the building. And then by using mathematical calculations, they can calculate the angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we play on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Pause there, please. We're at 5 minutes and 32 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What is taking place at this point of the video?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: From the shape of the shrapnel marks in the tarmac, this soldier is now looking at the direction from which the round has come and now taking his bearing using the compass.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. And we are -- would you agree that this isn't necessarily a video of the entire investigative process, taking the direction or taking the height?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: It doesn't seem to be. This video only captures, obviously, certain parts of the total investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we play on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could pause there, please. We're at 6 minutes and 28 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What is taking place at this stage?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: They're now doing a preliminary investigation on the tail-fins from the round. This is where they can find certain information. You can just see it in the video, where the mark and batch number are stamped on the rear. And they have laid the tape measure down to measure the distance across the fins just to confirm the calibre of the mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We can play on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We can stop the video at this stage. Thank you. I have no further questions in examination-in-chief. I was going to seek the admission of the documents as well as the video at this stage, or I can do that at the end of the evidence of the witness, as Your Honours wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have no objection to the admission as source documents, pursuant to the Trial Chamber's decision on the Prosecution's submission on the relevancy of certain documents relating to the testimony of Richard Philipps on the 9th of July, 2010. But as you noted in paragraph 11, the substance of those documents should not be considered by the Chamber, only to the extent of assisting the Chamber in assessing the probative value of the expert testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're tendering these documents to be admitted for all purposes, in accordance with the guidance which is set out in the decision that Mr. Robinson has referred to. These are not merely admitted as source documents. The witness has had an opportunity to comment upon them, to explain their relevance to the Chamber. And in the same way as Your Honours admitted for all purposes documents admitted through Expert Donia, we are tendering these documents for all purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the problem that -- I think we, in principle, could understand to have these documents admitted for all purposes if we had the opportunity for a robust cross-examination of all of these incidents. But given the time that the Chamber has allowed for cross-examination, to have documents admitted as to the substance of the investigation, without having the ability to question those people who conducted the investigation, would really prejudice us, given the time. However, if we have enough time for a robust cross-examination of each of these incidents, then we really wouldn't mind the documents, themselves, being admitted. But given the Chamber's philosophy towards the evidence of this witness, as reflected in the time allowed for cross-examination, we don't feel that it would be fair to admit these for all purposes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a break for half an hour, and we'll give our ruling afterward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is our ruling: The Chamber has considered the arguments put forward by Mr. Robinson as to why the underlying investigatory reports and other material reviewed by Mr. Higgs, in reaching his conclusions and preparing his report, should be admitted as source documents rather than for all purposes, as the Prosecution wishes. However, as this underlying material was referred to by the witness in the course of his testimony, the situation differs from that of Mr. Philipps and the source material that was only referenced in his expert report and not discussed in the courtroom with him. Having said that, as we indicated in our ruling on the time for cross-examination of Mr. Higgs, the Chamber is of the view that his evidence is of a limited nature, as he could only comment, on the basis of his expertise, on the investigations conducted by others and the conclusions reached by them. This has an effect on the weight which the Chamber can ascribe to those underlying reports and other materials, and, indeed, there would need to be further evidence brought to support them before the Chamber could reach conclusions based thereon. As he's not the author of these underlying reports, additional time to cross-examine this witness about them would be of limited purpose, and the Chamber remains of the view that three hours is sufficient. With these comments, the Chamber will admit the documents commented upon by the witness in the course of his testimony and upon which he based his expert report. That was the ruling, and I was told that there's something to be raised by Mr. Gaynor or Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I wanted to raise one scheduling issue that I had an opportunity to speak with the Defence about. The Court will be aware that there were three witnesses scheduled for this week. A look at the allotted -- the cross-examination times consumed and allotted thus far suggests the possibility that we may complete the testimony of those three witnesses before the completion of the week. It remains the expectation and certainly the preference, strong preference, to the parties, as I gleaned during the course of a discussion during the recess, to maintain the existing schedule, that is, three witnesses this week, and then commence with KDZ-088 on Monday. I see the Court may be in agreement with that, and I won't continue if that's the case, but I wanted to alert the Court to that position so that the Bench was as aware of the circumstances as possible and could provide whatever relevant feedback it shows so there'd be as much certainty possible. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Thank you for the information. What I wanted to tell you is that not to make the final arrangement to call KDZ-88 on Monday. The reason will become apparent by the course of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour. And may I take this opportunity to raise a related matter, and that would be to encourage the Court, to the extent it may be possible, to provide the parties with as much advance notice of allotted -- of cross-examination time to be allotted as it can. And that means, if possible, as many witnesses ahead as possible. The reasons are obvious. I appreciate the burdens involved, but it would be of great benefit to the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll do so. Let's bring in the witness. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although the Trial Chamber concluded that the evidence provided by Mr. Higgs does require further testimony, I'm afraid that through his testimony these reports are being legitimised to a considerable degree. I kindly ask you to consider the necessity of having more time before KDZ-88 arrives. I would like to deal with 80 incidents that Mr. Higgs dealt with, major incidents, at that. We will not have a better opportunity of clarifying the matter than the opportunity that is at hand now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber gave its ruling, and we are not minded to revisit the issue. Read again the ruling we gave, and comply with it as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's begin your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Higgs. I'd like to express to you my gratitude for meeting with the Defence team and also for your promise that you would give us a list of your previous testimony and involvement in criminal cases in the UK and other countries. We will ask to refer to some of these cases to understand your method of work. Do you agree that your expertise is, in fact, a report on the work of other investigative teams, not an inquiry into the incidents themselves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: In these cases, my reports are based on the investigations carried out by others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But in the course of our interview, you said, I have to believe that -- [In English] that I based my opinion on -- through ... [Interpretation] And you said that one must hope that they are correct.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I must believe what was written in those investigations was done correct at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you would agree, wouldn't you, that in order for us to check the veracity of your own conclusions, whereby you lend credibility to their findings, we have only one course of action open, and that is to clear up these incidents, themselves, with your assistance here; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I can give you my opinion on each of these incidents here to enable them to be cleared up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now ask for the video, 65 ter 40221.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we need to switch to Sanction again? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need the sequence of minute and 25 seconds. Rewind a little, please. One minute, 20. 1:25. 1:25. Can you freeze there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Higgs, that in a human body there is more than two-thirds of liquid; blood, lymph, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I'm obviously no doctor. I'm led to believe that, but I obviously could not give a definite answer on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get that picture back? Where is that picture?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you explain how this body found itself there and how these wounds were inflicted?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Difficult to confirm exactly how it ended there, as I can only see the pictures as you can. It would look like this person has been caught within the blast or shrapnel of the round, causing the injuries, and then pushing -- the blast pushing the individual over the barrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you explain where are his bodily fluids that must have flowed out of the body with an injury like this? Where are they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Well, all I can see on this picture is, as you can, where the blood-stains are on the side of the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the asphalt below the body is dry?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: From the quality of the picture, I cannot see large quantities, but I couldn't rule out there being some.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you notice the shadow of the body?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the shadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call -- can we now see the sequence of 3:43, the arrival of the French team. Is this it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's the French investigative team, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that the first team to appear on the scene?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I don't know if these were the first. The video doesn't either confirm or deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During our interview, you confirmed that the best time to investigate an incident is immediately after it occurred; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 4:37.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are these members of the French Battalion measuring the crater?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: No, they're not measuring the crater. They're measuring the distance from the crater to the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. They're measuring the position relative to the building?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we see here a clear image of the crater?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Not in this image, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we rewind a few seconds. We can play the footage now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this a better picture?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: It is, but it still does not show the crater in any great detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can it be seen that the crater, the traces, are marked by chalk?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: It's not clear to see, from the picture, whether or not they are marked by chalk or whether that is just white edges to the splinters in the tarmac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we play the film now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us listen carefully to what this man using the compass will say. You can play it back.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's freeze here. This French officer, did he say "2.100"? Can the French interpreters help us? Did the French officer say "2.000 1.000 parts"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The French interpreters believe they heard "2.800 thousandths."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... the officer said "2.000 1.000 parts."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was advised by the interpreter that the French booth believes that they heard "2.800 --" "2.800 thousandths."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we rewind again and listen once again carefully to what the officer said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if the French interpreters could interpret what they hear in French.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Please write down, Cherry. Are you there? Note down bearing 2.800 thousandths."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can we now move to 6:28.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Higgs, that on this stabiliser there is no -- no ignition device, detonator?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The ignition device for this tail-fin, you can clearly see it's in the picture. It is in the center. That is a percussion cap that is in the center of the tail-fin, which fires the round. Obviously, if you're referring to the fuse, of course, that would be on the opposite end of the round, which detonates on impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if we look at the place where a brass cap should be, the one that activates the motor, not the shell, it activates the charge, and it's made of brass or at least it's the colour of brass, made of a soft material?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Not on all mortar rounds the percussion caps are made of brass or copper. Sometimes they are made of a silver-coloured alloy. It would depend on the type and batch of ammunition. And sometimes these can even be displaced after firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We accept, don't we, that it's missing here in this picture? It had been released earlier or it's missing. But do you know from what material Yugoslav-made detonator caps are made; a coloured metal or a colourless metal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Two questions there. The first one regarding it being missing: No, I can't confirm that because it could be -- still be in place. This photograph is not clear enough to show that. Regarding the colour and this type of batch of ammunition: No, I have not got that detail information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue with the play-back, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Freeze. We had a sharper picture of the body of the stabiliser a moment ago. Can we rewind a few seconds, perhaps. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What would you say about the body of this stabiliser? Are these traces of explosion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The stabiliser shows the damage that would be consistent with being fired, as you can see from the end of the stabiliser nearest to the right-hand edge of the screen, where it has been peeled back from firing. And the tail-fins represent a tail-fin that has, since the explosion, hit something and, therefore, caused damage to the fins.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see that the emplacement of the detonator cap is empty? Can you see that now?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Again, I'm not really clear enough to see that, because on firing they will be pressed in by the firing pin. So this is not clear enough to either confirm or disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has this video been admitted into evidence? Wasn't it tendered by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, our understanding is that it's been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why does it bear this different number?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry. The video has been admitted in evidence. The stabiliser --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, the video you played is numbered as 40310, and this one was referred to as 40221.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm informed that they are duplicates of each other and this is the correct number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the correct number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That one has been already admitted, and the exhibit number will be assigned by the Court Deputy in due course. I take it it should be probably P1450.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now get 1D2253.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we switch to e-court from Sanction?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the photograph I wanted. Can we restore it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is a photo of the Markale Market-Place? This is a freeze taken from pre-war video footage shown on TV. And do you agree that this is the Markale Market, covered by some sort of roofing plates that almost -- that are almost joined together, almost touch each other?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: From the picture, it does appear to be the market. However, obviously, I cannot definitely confirm that without seeing a bigger picture. But, yes, it does appear to be the Markale Market.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see the rails towards the bottom of the picture. Now, when you look at this photo and these big roofing plates, do you still stand by your finding, based on previous investigations, that it's possible, with one hit of this market, to land a shell without having the shell activate on the roofing plates?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, that is possible, because on the day of firing, of course, we do not know the position of these roofing plates, and the round could have quite easily passed in a gap between them. I obviously have no evidence or information to that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, as you were probably able to see in the material that the Muslim side gave you, it was the same location, the market looked the same, and it's documented in many photographs of Markale with covered stalls. Did you see such material? Did they give you all the background material you needed for your findings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: The findings, obviously, are based on the reports which are obviously in evidence. At no time I'm aware that they reported a round had passed through or hit one of these roofing covers. There was mention that it had, I think, hit a table on the way through, but I've got no evidence that I have seen which relates to these -- these covers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To make it quite clear for the participants in these proceedings, we're now talking about Markale I?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would a shell hitting these covers activate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Depending on what these covers are made of, how substantial they are, then, yes, it could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said, and we could see it in one UN report, that the shell hit a stall. Would it activate hitting a stall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: It depends on, of course, how it hit the stall and which part, but a stall could detonate it if it was hit correctly and with enough force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up 65 ter 10083. Before that, may I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless it is objected to, we'll admit this picture. Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Subject to the observation that we don't have any information as to when that photograph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was before the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: True. But beyond that, we're not given a year at all as to when that photograph might have been taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you help us in that regard, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I lived 50 years in this city, and I know it very well. This is what the Markale Market looked before -- just before the war and earlier, and this is a freeze from video footage shown on TV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's all you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With that caveat, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D542, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get 65 ter 10083.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's a part of your report, after touring the positions around Sarajevo, and this refers to your visit to Mrkovici village, located outside on the front-lines, behind the confrontation line on the Serbian side. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which part of the report are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The pages -- it's the last page: "I visited the area of Mirkovci ..." 0303-7515. Yes: "I have visited ..." Top of the page.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you mean by saying that there are several locations in Mrkovici that lend themselves to the placing of mortars, and there are access roads that can be used to transport them into Mrkovici?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: I was trying to establish all the possible locations where the round could have been fired from. With the 120-millimetre mortar, it is a heavy piece of equipment, a large piece of equipment, and certain areas then may not be suitable for the firing of that weapon system. So I was taken around to see different sites to see the possibilities of where it could have been located.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But during our interview you said that a mortar of 120 millimetres can be disassembled, shipped, and assembled again; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find, in Mrkovici, any sites where this heavy 120-millimetre mortar was dug in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Not sites that -- where it was dug in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you tour all the sites on that bearing between Mrkovici and Markale? Did you tour other places to see if there were any suitable sites for a mortar?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: We looked at all the area along that bearing line and identified the suitable places, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly look at the Map 02 from this special binder. That's the 02 from the Sarajevo special folder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't remember the 65 ter number of this, this picture, aerial image.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We're just getting it right now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm told it's 11790, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you show us Mrkovici on this map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Purely from this map -- obviously it's been some time since I have been there. I'm obviously now no longer really familiar with the named areas. So it would really be not accurate for me now trying to determine which -- where exactly this area is on this particular aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it's easier in the lower part of the city. Can you show Markale on this picture?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Well, the lower part of the city, of course, shows here where the airport is. Of course, Markale is at the other end of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the eastern part of the city, this narrowest part of the city, do you see the main street winding through the old town?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Not clearly on this photograph, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Markale are in the old town?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, they're in the old town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that when you go from the old town towards the top, towards this mountain, that Mrkovici are behind the confrontation line, to the north of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Without checking that against a map showing the areas with the names on, obviously, I cannot show it on this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll show that map later as well. But do you agree that the confrontation lines are very close together in this section?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS
utterances.text: Yes, that picture does show the confrontation lines are very close together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that will be it for today. So we'll rise, and we'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. Mr. Higgs, probably you will know very well that during the course of your testimony, you are not supposed to discuss your evidence with anybody else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: See you tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 19th day of August, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 25
